title: Bond Energies
content:
# Bond Energies

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Define bond energy
- Explain energy changes in terms of bond breaking and making
- Use bond energies to calculate enthalpy changes
- Explain why bond energy values are averages

## Introduction

**Bond energy** is the energy needed to break a specific chemical bond. Understanding bond energies allows us to calculate the energy change for any reaction, even without performing experiments.

## Key Concepts

### What is Bond Energy?

**Bond energy:** The energy required to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules.

Units: **kJ/mol**

**Important points:**
- Breaking bonds is **endothermic** (requires energy)
- Making bonds is **exothermic** (releases energy)
- Bond energies are always **positive** (energy is always needed to break bonds)

### Bond Breaking and Making

**During any chemical reaction:**
1. Bonds in reactants must be **broken** (energy absorbed)
2. New bonds in products are **formed** (energy released)

**Overall enthalpy change:**
$$\Delta H = \text{Energy to break bonds} - \text{Energy released making bonds}$$

Or:
$$\Delta H = \sum \text{Bond energies (broken)} - \sum \text{Bond energies (formed)}$$

### Common Bond Energies

| Bond | Bond energy (kJ/mol) |
|------|---------------------|
| H-H | 436 |
| O=O | 498 |
| N≡N | 945 |
| C-H | 413 |
| C-C | 347 |
| C=C | 614 |
| C≡C | 839 |
| C=O | 805 |
| C-O | 358 |
| O-H | 464 |
| N-H | 391 |
| C-N | 286 |
| C-Cl | 346 |
| H-Cl | 432 |
| H-Br | 366 |
| Cl-Cl | 243 |
| Br-Br | 193 |

**Note:** Double bonds (=) are stronger than single bonds (-)
Triple bonds (≡) are stronger than double bonds (=)

### Why Are Bond Energies Averages?

**Example - C-H bond:**
- In CH₄ (methane): C-H = 435 kJ/mol
- In C₂H₆ (ethane): C-H = 421 kJ/mol
- In CH₃OH (methanol): C-H = 402 kJ/mol

The exact bond energy depends on the molecular environment.

**Average bond energy:** The mean of bond energies measured in many different molecules.

This is why calculated ΔH values may differ slightly from experimental values.

### Calculating Enthalpy Changes

**Method:**
1. Draw out the structural formulas showing all bonds
2. Count all bonds broken (in reactants)
3. Count all bonds formed (in products)
4. Calculate: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed)

**If ΔH is negative:** Exothermic (more energy released than absorbed)
**If ΔH is positive:** Endothermic (more energy absorbed than released)

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Calculate the enthalpy change for the combustion of hydrogen:
$$\text{2H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{2H}_2\text{O}$$

Bond energies: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, O-H = 464 kJ/mol

**Solution:**

**Bonds broken (in reactants):**
- 2 × H-H = 2 × 436 = 872 kJ
- 1 × O=O = 1 × 498 = 498 kJ
- Total energy in = **1370 kJ**

**Bonds formed (in products):**
- 4 × O-H (two water molecules) = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ
- Total energy out = **1856 kJ**

**Enthalpy change:**
$$\Delta H = 1370 - 1856 = -486 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

The reaction is **exothermic** (ΔH is negative).

---

**Example 2:** Calculate ΔH for the reaction:
$$\text{CH}_4 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

Bond energies: C-H = 413, Cl-Cl = 243, C-Cl = 346, H-Cl = 432 (all kJ/mol)

**Solution:**

**Bonds broken:**
- 1 × C-H = 413 kJ
- 1 × Cl-Cl = 243 kJ
- Total = **656 kJ**

**Bonds formed:**
- 1 × C-Cl = 346 kJ
- 1 × H-Cl = 432 kJ
- Total = **778 kJ**

**Enthalpy change:**
$$\Delta H = 656 - 778 = -122 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

The reaction is **exothermic**.

---

**Example 3:** Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane:
$$\text{CH}_4 + \text{2O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O}$$

Bond energies: C-H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O-H = 464 (all kJ/mol)

**Solution:**

**Bonds broken:**
- 4 × C-H = 4 × 413 = 1652 kJ
- 2 × O=O = 2 × 498 = 996 kJ
- Total = **2648 kJ**

**Bonds formed:**
- 2 × C=O (in CO₂) = 2 × 805 = 1610 kJ
- 4 × O-H (in 2H₂O) = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ
- Total = **3466 kJ**

**Enthalpy change:**
$$\Delta H = 2648 - 3466 = -818 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

This is close to the experimental value of -890 kJ/mol. The difference is because bond energies are averages.

---

**Example 4:** The enthalpy change for breaking the N≡N bond is +945 kJ/mol. What does this tell you about the bond?

**Solution:**
- The N≡N bond has a high bond energy
- This means it is a very strong bond
- A lot of energy is needed to break it
- This is why nitrogen gas (N₂) is so unreactive
- The triple bond makes nitrogen very stable

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to count ALL bonds (including multiple bonds of the same type)
- **Correct:** Draw structural formulas and count every single bond

- **Mistake:** Getting the formula the wrong way around
- **Correct:** ΔH = bonds broken - bonds formed (not formed - broken)

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that bond breaking is endothermic
- **Correct:** Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases energy

## Practice Questions

1. Define the term 'bond energy'. (2 marks)

2. Explain why breaking bonds is an endothermic process. (2 marks)

3. Use bond energies to calculate ΔH for:
   $$\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2HCl}$$
   Bond energies: H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 243, H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol (3 marks)

4. Use bond energies to calculate ΔH for:
   $$\text{N}_2 + \text{3H}_2 \rightarrow \text{2NH}_3$$
   Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H-H = 436, N-H = 391 kJ/mol (4 marks)

5. Explain why calculated enthalpy changes using bond energies may differ from experimental values. (3 marks)

6. The C=C bond energy is 614 kJ/mol and the C-C bond energy is 347 kJ/mol. Explain why the C=C bond energy is not exactly twice the C-C bond energy. (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Bond energy | Energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond |
| Average bond energy | The mean bond energy measured across many compounds |
| Bond breaking | An endothermic process (absorbs energy) |
| Bond making | An exothermic process (releases energy) |

## Summary

- **Bond energy** = energy to break one mole of a bond (kJ/mol)
- **Breaking bonds:** endothermic (energy in)
- **Making bonds:** exothermic (energy out)
- **Formula:** ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed)
- If ΔH negative → exothermic
- If ΔH positive → endothermic
- Bond energies are **averages** - actual values vary with environment
- Stronger bonds = higher bond energy (e.g., N≡N = 945 kJ/mol)
- Double/triple bonds are stronger than single bonds
